story.headline: Djokovic exits US Open in first round
story.summary: Novak Djokovic lost his US Open opener to Mariano Navone, his first ever first-round exit at Flushing Meadows, breaking down in tears.
story.display_body: Novak Djokovic, the 24-time Grand Slam champion and fourth seed, lost his opening match to Argentina's Mariano Navone 7–6 (7–5) 5–7 4–6 6–2 6–1, breaking down in tears in the deciding set of a match in which he struggled physically throughout — he was seen vomiting into a courtside bin. It is the first time in 20 appearances that Djokovic has lost in the first round at the US Open (he had won all 19 previous openers), and his first opening-round defeat at any Grand Slam since 2006. The 39-year-old, chasing a record 25th major, congratulated the 25-year-old Navone on the biggest win of his career.
story.why: This is the clearest evidence yet that the last man standing from tennis's "Big Three" is being caught by time — and it landed the day after his greatest rival was formally enshrined in the sport's history.

story.headline: Federer inducted into Tennis Hall of Fame
story.summary: Swiss great Roger Federer was tearfully inducted into the International Tennis Hall of Fame at Newport.
story.display_body: Switzerland's Roger Federer was inducted into the International Tennis Hall of Fame, calling it "one of the greatest honours" of his life. The 20-time Grand Slam singles champion, who retired in 2022, was tearful at the Newport ceremony in front of greats including Billie Jean King and John McEnroe. Federer won a record eight Wimbledon titles, six Australian Opens, five US Opens and one French Open, and spent 310 weeks as world number one — the mark later surpassed by Djokovic.
story.why: A Swiss sporting icon receives tennis's ultimate lifetime recognition — and the timing, one day before Djokovic's collapse in New York, underlined how completely one era is giving way to the next.

story.headline: Young Boys and Basel draw 3-3
story.summary: Swiss Super League heavyweights Young Boys and Basel drew 3-3 in round five, leaving the title race congested.
story.display_body: The season's two heavyweights met at Bern's Wankdorf on Saturday and produced a six-goal stalemate: Young Boys 3–3 Basel, neither side able to land the decisive blow. That leaves Young Boys unbeaten but held, and hands the early initiative to the week's quieter stories — Lugano won 2–1 at Sion to stretch a winning run to four, while defending champions Thun (crowned for the first time in the club's history last season) rallied to win 4–3 away at St. Gallen, who lost for the first time. Promoted Vaduz thrashed Grasshoppers 5–2 for a maiden win of the campaign, Zürich won at Lausanne, and ten-man Luzern clung on for a 1–1 draw at Servette. Five rounds in, the title picture is congested rather than settled.
story.why: The two clubs most Swiss fans expect to contest the title spent 90 minutes proving how even the top of the table is — good news for a league that wants a race, not a procession.

story.headline: Fernandes hat-trick sparks Man Utd comeback
story.summary: Bruno Fernandes scored a hat-trick as Manchester United came from behind to beat Ipswich 5-2 as the transfer window neared its deadline.
story.display_body: Manchester United trailed Ipswich Town before Bruno Fernandes scored a hat-trick in a 5–2 comeback win — a marker of intent for Michael Carrick's rebuild, on a day when Marcus Rashford made his first Premier League start for the club since December 2024 and teenager Kobbie Mainoo returned to the side. Chelsea, meanwhile, kept a perfect start with a seven-goal thriller against Brighton. The bigger backdrop is the calendar: the summer transfer window shuts at the start of September, and the marquee confirmed departure is Ollie Watkins, Aston Villa's record Premier League scorer (91 goals), completing a £51m move to Al-Hilal of the Saudi Pro League on a three-year deal.
story.why: Two early-season statements from clubs with title ambitions — and a reminder that Saudi money is still strong enough to pull a 30-year-old England international out of the Premier League at his peak.

story.headline: FIA lifts Russia ban, Ukraine complains
story.summary: The FIA lifted its ban on Russian and Belarusian competitors, prompting a formal ethics complaint from Ukraine's motorsport federation.
story.display_body: Motorsport's governing body, the FIA, has lifted the ban on Russian and Belarusian competitors in international events — a ban in place since Russia's February 2022 invasion of Ukraine. The move, approved by the FIA's World Council and reportedly proposed by president Mohammed Ben Sulayem, drew an immediate formal complaint to the FIA ethics committee from the Ukrainian Automobile Federation (FAU), which is demanding an urgent investigation of its Russian counterpart. The FAU says the Russian federation operates offices in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine — Crimea, Sevastopol, and the Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia regions, all UN-recognised as Ukrainian territory — in breach of FIA statutes that permit only one motoring club per country.
story.why: Sport keeps being asked to referee geopolitics. The FIA's decision would let Russian drivers back onto international grids while the war continues, and Ukraine is framing it as a governance breach rather than a sporting one.

story.headline: Norris extends McLaren deal to 2030
story.summary: Reigning world champion Lando Norris signed a contract extension with McLaren running to the end of 2030.
story.display_body: Reigning world champion Lando Norris has signed a contract extension keeping him at McLaren through the end of 2030, committing the sport's current benchmark driver to the constructors' champions for the long term.

story.headline: Pogacar out of Vuelta, Mas takes red jersey
story.summary: Race leader Tadej Pogacar abandoned the Vuelta after a stage-eight crash needing collarbone surgery; Enric Mas inherited the lead and won stage nine.
story.display_body: A week after the Vuelta a España — the third and final of cycling's three-week Grand Tours — opened with Tadej Pogačar in command, the world champion is out. Pogačar, the overwhelming favourite chasing the one Grand Tour missing from his career, crashed with about 33km left of Saturday's eighth stage and abandoned the race; his UAE Team Emirates doctor reported a broken left collarbone requiring surgery (delayed for concussion precautions), a concussion and a "stable" neck fracture. It is the first Grand Tour he has ever failed to finish. He had led by 3 minutes 50 seconds. Spain's Enric Mas inherited the leader's red jersey — declining to wear it on Saturday's podium out of respect — and then won Sunday's ninth stage atop the Aitana climb, extending his overall lead (the general classification, i.e. cumulative time) to 1:18 over Primož Roglič, with Félix Gall third and Britain's Oscar Onley up to fourth.
story.why: The most dominant stage racer of his generation was removed from a race he was strangling — and a Grand Tour that looked finished is suddenly a genuine contest with two weeks still to ride.

story.headline: Werro nears oldest world record in Zurich
story.summary: Swiss runner Audrey Werro clocked the third-fastest 800m in history at Weltklasse Zurich, closing on athletics' oldest outdoor world record.
story.display_body: On a record-breaking night at the Zurich Diamond League (the elite one-day meeting series), Swiss European champion Audrey Werro ran 1:53.70 over 800m — the third-fastest time in history — finishing just 0.42 seconds shy of Jarmila Kratochvilová's 1:53.28, set in 1983 and the oldest outdoor world record in athletics. Roared on by a 25,000-strong home crowd, the 22-year-old set a personal best and now holds four of the ten fastest 800m times ever run, all recorded this summer. She was not alone in threatening the history books: the same meeting produced two world records — Alison dos Santos in the 400m hurdles and Russell in the 100m hurdles.
story.why: A 43-year-old record that has outlasted whole eras of the sport now looks beatable, and a Swiss athlete on home soil is the one making it look inevitable — "sooner rather than later," in her own read of the race.

story.headline: Iran strikes US bases in Jordan and UAE
story.summary: Iran launched missiles and drones at US bases in Jordan and the UAE early on 31 August after a US strike on Larak Island, the first direct exchange since late July.
story.display_body: Iran fired missiles and drones at US bases in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates early on Monday 31 August, hours after a US strike on Iran's Larak Island — the first direct exchange between the two sides since late July and a sharp escalation in the six-month-old war. The United States said its forces hit two Iranian launchers on Larak Island, in the Strait of Hormuz (the narrow shipping chokepoint that carries roughly a fifth of the world's seaborne oil), on Sunday night 30 August. US Central Command (CENTCOM — the US military headquarters for the Middle East) characterised the operation as "limited, precise action against IRGC minelaying forces posing an imminent threat," and a US official told Al Jazeera the launchers were being readied to fire missiles carrying naval mines (underwater explosives that damage passing ships) toward the waterway. Iran's Revolutionary Guard (IRGC, its elite military branch) said the US attack killed and wounded soldiers and civilians, and Tehran's foreign ministry called it "a direct violation of national sovereignty." In response, the IRGC said it struck the King Hussein and Al Azraq bases in Jordan and the Al Menhad airbase in the UAE, calling the Jordan strikes "a legitimate exercise of self-defence" under the UN Charter. Jordan's army said it intercepted eight Iranian missiles that breached its airspace at dawn; the UAE said its air force downed a drone approaching from Iran but rejected Iran's claim that its airbase was hit; and a US official said the attack on Jordan was intercepted. President Masoud Pezeshkian said Iran was "not looking for war" but would "give a decisive response to the aggressors." President Donald Trump separately claimed on Truth Social that Iran's Kharg Island — its main oil-export terminal — was being "blown to smithereens," a claim Iran has not confirmed and that no independent source has verified.
story.why: after weeks in which Washington had shifted from air strikes toward economic pressure (last week's sanctions package it branded "Operation Economic Outcast"), the tit-for-tat strikes are exactly the collapse of the diplomatic off-ramp that US and regional mediators had been trying to avoid — and they drag Jordan and the UAE directly into a war that has already disrupted Gulf oil shipping.

story.headline: SCO summit opens in Bishkek
story.summary: Xi, Putin, Modi and Iran's Pezeshkian gathered in Bishkek for the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation's 25th-anniversary summit.
story.display_body: Leaders of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation opened a two-day summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, on Monday 31 August, with China's Xi Jinping, Russia's Vladimir Putin, India's Narendra Modi and Iran's Masoud Pezeshkian all attending as the bloc marks its 25th anniversary. The SCO — a Eurasian security and economic grouping whose members account for about 43% of the world's population and roughly a quarter of global output — is meeting under the motto "Together for Sustainable Peace, Development and Prosperity," with Turkey's Erdogan and UN Secretary-General António Guterres also expected. On the agenda: the US-Israel war on Iran, the Russia-Ukraine war, and — pointedly — new trade and transport corridors that route around chokepoints, including the North-South corridor linking Russia to India through Iran and Arctic shipping via the Northern Sea Route, after the Strait of Hormuz disruption snarled global supply chains. A Modi-Putin bilateral is scheduled, and India-China border talks remain live after last year's rapprochement. Analysts cautioned the bloc is less a coherent anti-Western alliance than a venue where states hedge against US power.
story.why: the optics of Xi, Putin and Modi in one room, days after US strikes on Iran, are a deliberate signal of a "multipolar" alternative to Western institutions — though analysts expect rhetoric to outrun any concrete deals.

story.headline: Nepal flood toll passes 900
story.summary: The death toll from the Nepal-Tibet Himalayan glacial flood passed 900 with more than 4,000 still missing.
story.display_body: The death toll from the Nepal-Tibet Himalayan flash flood passed 900 by Monday 31 August, with more than 4,000 people still reported missing, as Nepal issued a fresh flood warning that briefly halted rescue work. The disaster began on Wednesday 26 August when a glacier collapse sent ice, rock and mud down the valleys of Nepal's Rasuwa district and across the Tibetan border, and the toll has climbed steeply — from about 470 confirmed dead on Thursday 28 August to over 900 now, on both sides of the frontier. The UN said the impact is "immense": aid teams are working around the clock to reach communities cut off in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading; the WHO has warned of disease risk from displacement and disrupted water and sanitation; and UNICEF says 18 schools were destroyed and about 10,000 children need support to keep studying. A "barrier lake" (a natural dam of landslide debris) and renewed flood alerts continue to threaten a second surge, and the UN's disaster-risk chief called it a "mountain hazard event" unseen "for a very, very long time."
story.why: it is among the deadliest glacial-outburst floods on record, and with thousands still missing and the danger not yet past, both the toll and the humanitarian need are still rising.

story.headline: Iceland rejects EU accession talks
story.summary: Icelandic voters rejected resuming EU accession talks 52.8% to 47.2% in a referendum.
story.display_body: Icelanders rejected resuming European Union accession talks, with the "No" camp winning 52.8% to 47.2%, according to the official count published by public broadcaster RÚV over the weekend of 30 August. Turnout was 82% of the roughly 270,000 eligible voters in the nation of about 400,000, and the capital Reykjavík was the only area to back membership. Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir, who had campaigned for "Yes," called the result "a victory for democracy" rather than a setback and confirmed her government will not pursue accession "this term," instead deepening ties through the European Economic Area (the arrangement that already gives Iceland access to the EU single market without full membership — the same framework Switzerland has repeatedly debated). European Council President António Costa said the bloc "fully respects the democratic choice" and called Iceland "one of the EU's closest and most trusted partners." Iceland first applied in 2009 after the financial crisis and suspended talks in 2013; the left-leaning government elected in 2024 brought the referendum forward amid rising tension over Russia's war and US interest in Greenland, with fishing rights and sovereignty the decisive concerns.
story.why: it settles, at least for this parliament, a question Iceland has wrestled with for over a decade — and it is a data point Swiss readers will recognise, another small European state opting to keep the EU at arm's length via the EEA rather than join.

story.headline: Gunman kills woman at Aarau rave
story.summary: A gunman killed an Italian woman and wounded five people at the Aarauer Rave on 30 August, triggering an international manhunt.
story.display_body: A gunman opened fire on the crowd at the annual Aarauer Rave in the early hours of Sunday 30 August, killing a young Italian woman and wounding five other people aged 24 to 27, some seriously, and triggering a national and international manhunt. The shooting happened before 3 a.m. at the Schachen racecourse in Aarau (a town of about 22,300, some 40 km west of Zürich) where the techno party was being held; the attacker or attackers fled and police say they cannot yet confirm whether it was one person or several, or how they escaped. Aargau cantonal police, backed by the federal police office Fedpol, have opened the search through Europol and Interpol and sent liaison officers to Aarau; police in Freiburg, across the German border, are also assisting, and investigators have appealed for phone videos from the event. Italy's foreign ministry confirmed the dead woman was an Italian national and said it is following the Swiss investigation closely.
story.why: a fatal mass shooting at a public event is rare in Switzerland despite widespread gun ownership, and the cross-border manhunt underscores how quickly a cantonal crime became a European police operation.

story.headline: Swiss gender pay gap narrows again
story.summary: Swiss federal data show the overall gender pay gap fell to 15.7% in 2024, with an unexplained gap of 6.5% or 640 francs a month.
story.display_body: Switzerland's gender pay gap narrowed again in 2024, with women earning on average 15.7% less than men, down from 16.2% in 2022, the Federal Statistical Office (BFS) reported on Monday 31 August. The figure continues a long decline (18% in 2020, 19% in 2018) and is based on standardised gross monthly wages converted to full-time. Part of the gap reflects structural factors — education, seniority, management roles, sector — but comparing women and men with the same profile still leaves an "unexplained" gap of 6.5% across the whole economy, or about 640 francs gross per month, down from 7.0% (657 francs) in 2022. The unexplained gap varies widely: about 31% in banking and insurance versus roughly 8% in hospitality, and it is larger in small firms (8.6% under 20 employees), in senior management (12.4%), and for older and married women. The BFS notes that traits like marital status can describe wage differences but do not justify them.
story.why: the unexplained portion is the part that legal equal-pay obligations target, so its slow-but-steady shrinkage — and where it stays stubbornly high — is the concrete measure of whether Swiss equal-pay policy is working.

story.headline: Bund taps feed reserves in drought
story.summary: Switzerland released compulsory animal-feed reserves as a record heat and drought summer strains farms.
story.display_body: The federal government has released compulsory feed reserves to help livestock farmers, as a record-breaking heat and drought summer leaves pastures parched across Switzerland. The opening of the national stockpile (Pflichtlager) for animal feed is the latest sign of strain from a summer SRF and the weather service describe as record-breaking: reservoir levels are running below average, several cantons and cities have only just lifted or loosened forest fire bans, and some farmers have resorted to importing hay from as far as Canada to keep herds fed. Foresters warn that even healthy-looking trees risk sudden branch failure after the prolonged dryness.
story.why: tapping strategic reserves normally held for emergencies is a tangible measure of how far this summer's drought has pushed Swiss agriculture, and it points to higher feed costs and pressure on domestic food production heading into autumn.

fields.display_body: The federal government has released compulsory feed reserves to help livestock farmers, as a record-breaking heat and drought summer leaves pastures parched across Switzerland. The opening of the national stockpile (Pflichtlager) for animal feed is the latest sign of strain from a summer SRF and the weather service describe as record-breaking: reservoir levels are running below average, several cantons and cities have only just lifted or loosened forest fire bans, and some farmers have resorted to importing hay from as far as Canada to keep herds fed. Foresters warn that even healthy-looking trees risk sudden branch failure after the prolonged dryness.
